tom_tat: In the world, the Three Jewels is the most noble. Buddha Shakyamuni is Buddha Treasure. Three Pitakas of Disciplines by Buddha Shakyamuni...
noi_dung:
PrefaceIn the world, the Three Jewels is the most noble. Buddha Shakyamuni is Buddha Treasure. The three Pitakas of Vinaya Sutras expounded by Shakyamuni Buddha are the Dharma Jewels. Buddha's monastic disciples are Sangha Jewels. Buddha Shakyamuni entered Nirvana over twenty-five hundred years ago. The reason the Dharma torch of the Dharma Jewel is still propagated to this day is all due to the profound efforts of the sages and monks over many generations. With the spirit of great fearlessness, sacrificing their lives for the sake of Buddhism, from India and other countries in the Western Regions, they crossed the mountains of Tuyet Son and Thong Linh, or rode the waves of the South China Sea to spread and promote the teachings of Buddha to the East, without fearing many hardships and dangers.

On the path of propagating the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, depending on the base of each sentient being and depending on the needs of each country, from the three pure karma of body, speech and mind (i.e. body, speech, and mind), they flexibly use skillful means to save sentient beings. From pure mind karma, they self-cultivate the three subjects of anasrava, precepts, concentration and wisdom (i.e. mind teachings), which derive from the four majestic postures of pure body karma (i.e. body teachings), and use the good words of pure speech karma (i.e. oral teachings), to save sentient beings; That is to say, they often use majestic and simple gestures, use ascetic practice, use skillful words, use magical powers, and use Prajna wisdom to preach and translate the sutras, causing sentient beings everywhere to be imbued with the rain of dharma, to leave suffering and attain happiness, and to walk on the path of liberation.

Such is their great and noble grace, which is the driving force that motivates us to dedicate ourselves to translating their biographies, so that future generations will forever remember the extremely profound grace of the Sangha Treasure, and follow their example to progress on the path of karma and escape the cycle of birth and death.

In this book, we only compile translations about the lives of those who have made great contributions in spreading and translating the classics from the Later Han Dynasty to the end of the Tang Dynasty, that is, from the first to the tenth century, because that was the most important period of the work of translating the classics, along with the formation and development of sects in China, such as San Luan sect, Thanh That sect, Nirvana sect, Pure Land sect, Hoa Nghiem sect, Luat sect, Zen Buddhism, Phap Tuong Buddhism, Chan Ngon Buddhism, Cau Xa Buddhism, etc. These sects have deeply influenced Vietnamese Buddhism.

This book Thien Tang Thien Truc has reached readers largely thanks to the enthusiastic collaboration of friend Nguyen Van Sy.

Next, we sincerely pay our respects and prayers to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, saints and monks of the ten directions and three generations, and the great Venerable Master Tuyen Hoa to manifest their majesty and spirit to testify for this book. We also dedicate all our merits to pray for Vietnam and the World to be forever peaceful; Buddhism in Vietnam and the World will forever endure; All sentient beings in the Dharma world will soon attain Bodhi.

Finally, we sincerely hope that wise men will be merciful and forgive our sins and correct our mistakes and omissions in this book.

Namo Original Master Shakyamuni Buddha.

Thanh Thanh Temple of Ten Thousand Buddhas, America.

Bhikkhu Thich Hang Dat

Spring 1998.

tieu_de: 01. Venerable Nhiep Ma Dang (Kasyapa-Matanga, Kasyapa Ma Dang)
tom_tat: The Venerable was originally from Thien Truc (central India). Everyday gestures and charisma at all times reveal ecstasy, noble and gentle manners. For...
noi_dung:
01. Venerable Nhiep Ma Dang (Kasyapa-Matanga, Kasyapa Ma Dang)The Venerable was originally from Thien Truc (central India). Everyday gestures and charisma at all times reveal ecstasy, noble and gentle manners. Regarding the Mahayana and Hinayana sutras, the Venerable One always thoroughly understood the universal understanding. My lifelong wish is to always travel to different countries to save people.

One time, while preaching the Golden Light Sutra in a small country in Thien Truc, suddenly a foreign army invaded the palace, so the Venerable had to stop preaching the sutra. Ton Gia thought:

- Sutras often teach that if you often explain Buddhist scriptures, you will be protected by the earth god, and make your place of residence peaceful. Currently, war is breaking out. So is there any contrast with the above?

After thinking about it, the Venerable forgot all about the danger and quickly went to the two countries, calling on them to put down their weapons and stop fighting. Due to the Venerable's dignity, the two countries finally put aside their enmity and shook hands to make peace. Thanks to that, the Venerable's name resonated far and wide.

Han Ming De (58-75), in the reign of Vinh Binh, one night, dreamed of a strange omen. In his dream, he saw a golden body, more than six feet tall, his back emitting sunlight and moonlight, flying in the air, arriving in front of the palace. The next day, Han Ming De gathered all his officials to discuss the dream and see what it meant. Thai historian Pho Nghi, drew astrology and presented:

- During the time of King Zhou Chieu, the weather had a strange meteorology, with five-colored rays of light rotating on the Thai Vi star. At that time, the eunuch To Do said: 'There must be a saint, born in the West, that's why such auspicious omens appear in heaven. A thousand years later, the teachings of that saint will be transmitted to Central Earth.'

Hearing that, King Chu Chieu immediately ordered this matter to be engraved on stone, to make a stele passed down forever. Your Highness's dream last night, if calculated according to time, obviously has a close connection. Currently, I heard that in Tay Vuc there is a Buddha god. Your Highness, if you dream of a golden person, it must be Buddha.

Hearing this, Han Ming De sent a delegation of eighteen people such as mandarins Lang Trung, Tan Canh, Thai Ham, Doctor, Vuong Tuan, etc. led by Dau Co (grandson of Dau Dung, the first national-building minister of the Later Han Dynasty) to go to the country of Dai Nhuc Chi in Thien Truc, to search for Buddha Dharma. On the way to seek the Dharma, they met the Venerable, and they requested to go to Central Earth to propagate. The Venerable had a great wish to propagate the Dharma, so he accepted the request. Having gone through many hardships and dangers on the road, finally the Venerable along with a group of envoys used white horses to carry scriptures and returned to Luoyang. On that occasion, the king ordered the establishment of Bach Ma Pagoda in Lac Thanh, west of Ung Quan, to serve as a residence for Ton Gia. Trung Tho had monks starting from there.

Legend has it that this pagoda was originally named Chieu De, later changed to Bach Ma:

- Legend has it that foreign monarchs often brought troops to destroy pagodas, but only Chieu De pagoda has not been destroyed. One night, there was a white horse, circumambulating the pagoda's tower, roaring in sorrow. Hearing this, King Khai stopped destroying the pagodas, so from then on, Chieu De Pagoda was renamed Bach Ma Pagoda. The establishment of names of temples is often based on rules and regulations.

The above mentioned foreign monarchs are the Five Lakes monarchs who caused chaos in the Central Plains, but their names are difficult to know accurately. (Phap Bon Noi Truyen mentioned Bach Ma and Hung Thanh pagodas).

Han Phap Bon Internal Story says that after the Venerable Kasyapa Ma Dang arrived in Luoyang, the Taoists in the eighteen mountains at Ngu Nhac presented their petitions to King Han Minh De, on the first day of the first month, the 14th year of Vinh Binh. They wanted to compete with Buddhist monks in theory and magic. Emperor Han Ming then ordered the Song Tuong mandarin to instruct the two sects, Thich and Dao, to compete in magic at Bach Ma pagoda. Tru Thien Tin in Nam Nhac, Luu Chanh Niem in Hoa Nhac, Hoan Van Do in Hang Nhac, Tieu Dac Tam in Dai Nhac, Lu Hue Thong in Sung Nhac, along with 690 Taoists, set up three altars outside the pagoda: On the west altar, they arranged the Buddhist scriptures; In the middle of the altar, they display the royal scriptures; On the eastern side of the altar, they displayed a variety of food and objects to pray to the gods. Buddhist monks placed Buddha's relics and sutra statues on the west side of the road. Once the arrangements were complete, the Taoists recited the incantations and set fire to the altar but were unable to burn the scriptures. The harder they exerted themselves, the faster the fire went out. The Buddha's relics released five rays of light, flying in the air. Venerable Kasyapa Ma Dang flew up into the void and displayed many magical changes. Viewers were impressed. Liu Hue Thong and other Taoists, along with about 230 women in the inner palace, jointly vowed to become monks. The court then ordered the construction of ten pagodas; Use seven temples as temples for monks, and three temples as temples for nuns. The monks' pagoda was built outside Lac Duong citadel. The nuns' pagoda was established in Lac Duong citadel. The Taoists at Nam Nhac Mountain displayed all their talents, but their magic power was not equal to that of Buddhist monks, so they died in shame and anger.

After arriving in the Central Plains, the Venerable Kasyapa Ma Dang together with the Venerable Bamboo Phap Lan translated the Forty-Two Chapters Sutra, five volumes of the Buddha's Original Conduct Sutra, four volumes of the Ten Grounds of Ending Sutra, two volumes of the 260 Synergistic Precepts, one volume of the Hai Tang Dharma Sutra, and one volume of the Original Birth Sutra of the Buddha. Currently, only the Forty-Two Chapters Sutra still exists. Other sutras translated by the two monks were all lost due to fire and war. The Forty-Two Chapters of the Sutra is the first sutra translated from Sanskrit to Chinese by two venerable monks.

Legend has it that after being translated, this sutra was engraved into a stone chamber by the royal court, and then began to be passed down. The story told by the monk:

- First, this sutra was kept in the fourteenth Lan Dai stone chamber.

That Lan Dai, originally the forbidden library of the Later Han Dynasty. Later, Venerable Kasyapa Ma Dang passed away at Bach Ma Pagoda.

tom_tat: Ton Gia is also from Trung Thien Truc. The Venerable recited hundreds of thousands of chapters of the sutra. Before going to Dong Do, Venerable was once respected...
noi_dung:
02. Venerable Truc Phap Lan (Dharmaraksa)Ton Gia is also from Trung Thien Truc. The Venerable recited hundreds of thousands of chapters of the sutra. Before going to Dong Do, the Venerable was revered as a teacher by the scholars in Thien Truc.

The Venerable was originally a close Dharma friend of the Venerable Kasyapa Ma Dang, so he often traveled around the world, saving people. Later, at the request of the Han Dynasty envoys, Venerable along with Kashyapa Ma Dang went to Dong Do. However, contemporary scholars at Thien Truc all wanted to keep Venerable stay. Because he had a great wish to propagate Buddhism, the Venerable still went to Dong Do. After arriving in Lac Duong, the two monks Truc Phap Lan and Ca Diep Ma Dang were allowed by Han Minh De to reside at Bach Ma Pagoda. The two monks together translated the sutras as mentioned above. In addition, the Venerable Truc Phap Lan also translated the Manjushri Pure Law Sutra and the Ma Nghich Sutra by himself.

tom_tat: His name was originally An Tinh, but because he was the crown prince of An Tuc (Parthian), later generations called him An The Cao. For An...
noi_dung:
03. An The Cao (Parthamasiris)His name was originally An Tinh, but because he was the crown prince of An Tuc (Parthian), later generations called him An The Cao. Regarding An Tuc country, the history of the Pre-Han and Later Han dynasties, the Three Kingdoms period, the Northern and Southern dynasties, has clearly recorded. An Xi is the founder of the Arsakes nation. In the reign of Emperor Han Ming, the sixteenth year of Yongping (73), Ban Sieu served as an envoy to the Western Regions. During the reign of Emperor Han Hoa, the third year of Vinh Nguyen (91), Ban Sieu assumed the position of Cavalry Commander, dominating thirty countries in the Western Regions. During the Eastern Han dynasty, the reign of Zhanghe (87), the country of An Xi paid lion tribute to Central Earth. Again, in the reign of Duc Nien, the king of An Tu sent envoys to bring tribute to Trung Tho, opening the beginning of trade between the two countries. In the thirteenth year of Vinh Nguyen (101), the country of An Tu often brought gifts to pay tribute to the Eastern Han Dynasty. Forty-seven years later, An The Cao passed to Trung Tho.

To his parents, he was very filial, so he was praised by the people. His divine nature is very clear and diligent in studying, so he understands all foreign classics, the seven wonders (sun, moon, stars), the five elements, medicine, meteorology, and astronomy. Contemplating the person's appearance, he immediately knew the illness, then made medicine to treat the illness. Listening to the sounds of animals and birds, one can know their thoughts. One time, while walking on the road, suddenly a flock of swiftlets flew by. He told his companions:

- Those swiftlets said that soon someone will bring us food.

A moment later, it was indeed true. The people heard this and were amazed and admired Him. Therefore, his reputation from then on spread and shocked all countries in the Western Regions, and was revered by countries near and far.

When he was still at home studying Buddhism, he often strictly followed the precepts very carefully, without any distractions. He often gathered people together to preach sutras and preach the Dharma. As soon as his father passed away, he ascended the throne. At that time, the Kushan dynasty (Kushans, 78-320; founded the Dai Nhuc Chi kingdom) continuously conquered the countries in the west, and threatened the An Tu kingdom. Mr. An The Cao saw that the world was insecure, suffering was empty, and impermanent, so when it came to the throne, he was very frustrated with suffering. Therefore, after taking care of his father's burial, he ceded the throne to his uncle, then left home to study Buddhism, without any attachment to the throne, only diligently practicing. Fifty years after he passed away, the An Tu kingdom was destroyed because of a group of ministers competing for the throne.

After becoming a monk, he reviewed all the scriptures, among which the Abhidharma theory was very interesting. He often recited and maintained meditation sutras, so he always achieved wonderful things. Because he wanted to propagate Buddhism, he traveled all over the country, so he was very fluent in the languages ​​of those countries. Ta Phu of the Jin Dynasty wrote: "Gao Tong rejects customs, good people have the sound of the country", meaning that An The Cao clearly understood the different customs of each country and was fluent in the sounds of the languages ​​of those countries. Before going to Central Earth, when he was still in An Tuc country, until he came to the Western Regions, he was fluent in Chinese. During the reign of Han Emperor (147-167), around the age of thirty, he went through Dong Do to Truong An. With great talent and keen understanding, just by looking at something once, he immediately understands it. Upon arriving, he immediately began to propagate Buddhism, and translated many sutras, such as the An Ban Thu Y sutra, Am Tri Enter, the Great Twelve Gates, the Lesser Twelve Gates, etc.

Once upon a time, there was a Tripitaka shaman, from Thien Truc, named To Chung Ho, who wrote the essential meaning of the Sutra into twenty-seven chapters. An The Gao, based on that work, selected seven chapters and translated them into Chinese, which is today's 'Dao Dia' sutra. In total, he translated thirty-nine sutras. All the meanings are clear and clear, and the writing is very precise. Although the writing is not flowery, the body is not rudimentary.

Mr. An The Cao often talked about his strange karma in previous lives that others could not understand. He said that in his previous life he was also a monk. At that time, he had a fellow practitioner with a very hot temper. When he met a donor who did not please him, he became angry. No matter how many times he advised, that monk's character remained the same. More than twenty years later, An The Cao said goodbye to that monk and said:

- I have to go to Guangzhou to repay the debt in my previous life. He has a profound understanding of the sutras and is diligent and diligent. However, because the Master's nature is full of resentment, after giving up his retribution, he will receive the form of an evil spirit. If I realize the results, I will definitely save you from disaster.

Having finished speaking, Mr. An The Cao then went to Guangzhou. At that time, that area was in chaos and bandits emerged like bees. In the middle of the road, he met a young man coming from afar. That young man then took out his knife and said:

- Ah! I came here to give My life!

He said:

- In my previous life, I owed you my life, so I traveled many miles to come here to repay you. As soon as he saw me, he immediately felt anger. This is because the grudge has not been resolved yet!

Having finished speaking, he calmly presented his head to be beheaded, without the slightest expression of fear. Without any delay, the young man swung his knife and beheaded him. At that time, his consciousness flew through the country of An Tuc and was also reincarnated as the crown prince, that is, the current An The Cao.

Towards the end of the Han Dynasty, eunuchs fought for power. When Emperor Ling of Han died, Dong Zhuo (?-192) led a large army into Luoyang. Fighting broke out constantly. Therefore, An The Cao had to leave Luoyang city and go to Jiangnan region to continue spreading the Dharma. He said to himself:

- First, I have to go to Lo Son, to save my fellow Dharma students from previous lives.

When he arrived at Lo Son, he resided at Dinh Ho hermitage. According to Mr. Hue Vien (334-417), in the book 'Lo Son Luoc Ky', it is written as follows: "At the top of the southern mountain, under Lam Cung Dinh lake, there is a temple of gods, which should be used for the royal court. The gods at Cung Dinh Ho temple were transformed by An The Cao. The story is still recorded in Tu Son Bac Thien."

Legend has it that Cung Dinh Ho temple is very strange. Merchants traveling back and forth to that area must first pray and worship to be safe. A certain guy sneaked up the mountain to cut bamboo, but refused to go to the temple to worship. As soon as that guy's bamboo boat left the river wharf, it was overturned by waves and sank. The merchants saw this and worshiped the temple even more.

One day, Mr. An The Cao followed more than thirty merchants on a boat to go to that temple. Upon arriving, the merchants went into the temple to worship, while He was on the boat. After they finished offering their offerings to pray for peace, the god in the temple told them:

- There is a monk on the boat, so please invite him here.

The merchant was horrified when he heard this, so he quickly ran out to invite him into the temple. As soon as he entered, he heard the god say:

- In my past life, I once became a monk and practiced Buddhism in the Western Regions. Although he often gives alms, he has a lot of anger, so he became a god at this Cung Dinh Ho temple. The temple's circumference of a thousand miles is all under my control. Because in my previous life I often practiced almsgiving, I have now received countless priceless treasures. However, due to anger, he received the retribution of becoming an evil devil, with a large and ugly body. My life is about to end. At death, the body will release a foul odor throughout rivers and lakes. Therefore, I had to go to a stream in the western mountains to die. After death, one will fall into hell and experience suffering. Please be merciful, bring all the precious objects to make offerings to the Three Jewels on my behalf, and build temples together, so that in my next life I will be reborn in a good realm.

Hearing these words, Mr. An The Cao said:

- I originally came here to save you. Why don't you show your true form?

God replied:

- I originally had the form of an evil devil. If he appeared, the people would certainly be frightened and frightened.

- Just showing up is enough. People are not afraid.

From inside the temple, a large bamboo boat appeared and crawled next to An The Cao. He then preached the Dharma and recited mantras in Sanskrit. Later, I felt a stream of emotions pouring out like rain, then slowly disappeared. He then picked up the precious treasures, then returned to the boat with the merchants. At that time, everyone saw the bamboo boat appear in its original form on the top of the western mountain, its body several miles long. At sunset, the boat was gliding on the river when suddenly a young man appeared and bowed his head to pay homage to him. After receiving his blessing, the young man suddenly disappeared. He told the merchants:

- That young man was originally from the Dinh Ho temple. Now he has escaped from evil and ascended to heaven.

Palace Dinh Ho Temple has no longer been sacred since then. Later, local people discovered the body of a huge bamboo boat, several miles long, lying in a stream to the west of Lo Son mountain. Currently, that mountainous area is called Xa Thon, Tam Duong district, in Jiangxi.

The Autobiography Tower records: "Ngoa Quan Pagoda in Don Duong was founded by the monk Hue Lap during the reign of Jin Ai De. Later, the monk An The Cao brought remnants from the Ho Palace to repair."

After paying back part of his karma, he also went to the Guangzhou area, found the young man who killed him in his previous life, and recounted his past life's fate, to let go of the past injustice, hoping to form a friendship together. When they met face to face, He said to that person:

- I also have a debt that I haven't paid yet. Now we have to go there and pay it back.

That person knew that he was not an ordinary person, so he respectfully made offerings. The next day, he and that person went out to the street and saw two guys fighting with sticks. A guy suddenly hit Him on the head by mistake, causing Him to die. Seeing the cause and effect retribution twice, that person then develops a diligent mind to practice Buddhism, and also often tells this true story to others. Anyone who hears this story will deeply believe in the principle of cause and effect and retribution in three lifetimes.

Sanskrit and Chinese are very different. However, the scriptures he translated were easy for everyone to read.

In the Tripitaka, An The Gao's disciple Nghiem Phat Dieu wrote the foreword to the book 'The Samaritan Thap Hui Chuong Cu'. He highly praised the merits of his guru. Venerable Khuong Sang Hoi (217-280) praised An The Gao in the preface to the sutra 'An Ban Thu Y'. Tran Hue proclaimed An The Cao as Bodhisattva Universal View in the preface to the Amitabha Sutra. Mr. Dao An (312-385) also highly praised Mr. An The Cao in the preface to the 'An Ban Thu Y' sutra, and often said:

- If you meet Mr. An The Cao, it will be like meeting a saint.

According to Mr. Dao An, Mr. An The Gao continuously translated the classics for twenty-two years, from the reign of Han Hoan De (148) to the reign of Han Linh De (169). In addition, in the prefaces to the Great Twelve Doors Sutra, the Path, etc., the great monks of the time praised An The Cao's merits.

Nghiem Phat Dieu once wrote: "All the places of An The Cao's entry and exit, either explained by word of mouth, or transmitted by writing."

Using his mouth to explain means he often expounds the scriptures. Using the written word to transmit means he translated the sutras from Sanskrit into Chinese.

In the past, Buddhism was introduced to East India very early. Folk also know how to worship Buddhism. Furthermore, there were also many monks from the Western Regions who came to translate the sutras, but most of them did not clearly state the name of the sutras, and even the identity of the translator was not available. It was not until the reign of Han Ming De that the court officially acknowledged the translation of the sutra by the two monks Kasyapa Ma Dang and Truc Phap Lan. However, talking about history, An The Gao was the first translator of the classics.

Two hundred years after An Shigao passed away, in the Eastern Jin Dynasty, Dao An (312-385) composed a table of contents of the classics. The next person followed that and wrote the book 'Exit Tripitaka', segmenting and recording the names of ancient translators. According to the book 'Exit Tripitaka', An Thegao translated thirty-four volumes, and forty volumes of sutras as follows: Sutra of An Ban Thu Y (1 volume), Amitabha Sutra (1 volume), Hundred Six and Ten Phams (1 volume), Great Twelve Gates (1 volume), Lesser Twelve Mons (1 volume), Great Path to the Ground (2 volumes), Origin of Human Desires (1 volume), Path of Intention Hanh (2 volumes), Abhidhamma Five Dharmas (1 volume), Seven Dharmas (1 volume), Five Dharmas (1 volume), Ten Dharmas (2 volumes), Universal Dharma Meaning (1 volume), Meaningful Law (1 volume), Laufenpo (1 volume), Four Truths (1 volume), Seven Places and Three Contemplations (2 volumes), Nine Hengs (1 volume), Noble Eightfold Path (1 volume), Miscellaneous Sutras of the Fourteen Heavens (2 volumes), Five Ten Teachings (2 volumes), Dai An Ban Thu (1 volume), Thoughts (1 volume), Twelve Causes and Conditions (1 volume), Five Aggregates (1 volume), Zhuan Dharma Wheel (1 volume), Liu Nhiep (1 volume), Thi Phap Phi Dharma (1 volume), Phap Tho Tran (1 volume), Fourteen Intentions (1 volume), Basic Generals of Medicine and Will (1 volume), Abhidhamma Nine Seven Paramitas (1 volume), Meditation on the Dharma Thought (1 volume), Nande Ca La Viet (1 volume).

The content of the sutras that Mr. An The Cao translated, the summary is divided into two parts: The first is the type of sutra that belongs to contemplative meditation, such as the sutra on Dai An Giving Attention, Meditation on Action, Dharma Thought, etc. The second type is according to number dharma, such as the sutra on Amitabha Sutra, Four Truths, Noble Eightfold Path, Five Dharmas, Twelve Causes and Conditions, etc.

The sutra representing meditation is the An Ban Thu Y sutra. The content of this sutra has ten points: Instantiation, perception, concentration, contemplation, completeness, purity, and the four truths.

1/ Ganana means counting breaths. 2/ Depending on the thoughts (anugama) is depending on the breath in and out without the mind wandering. 3/ Just (sthana) is to stop the mind and meditate. 4/ Contemplation (upalaksana) is to observe the realm clearly. 5/ Complete (vivartana) is also called turning, that is, reflecting and contemplating the mind, knowing clearly that it is not real. 6/ Purity (parisuddhi) is the mind that has no refuge and does not give rise to false thoughts. Adding the four truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and path, creates ten points for developing wisdom. The An Ban Thu Yin Sutra was established due to these ten points of wisdom. However, this sutra stands out in the first six points. Based on these six points, later the great master Tri Gia (538-596) of the Thien Thai sect founded the Luc Dieu Dharma Mon. These six types are entered by the book of contemplation; Slowly regulate your breathing, and count your breaths in and out, to make your mind focus in one place, that is, practice the method of calm meditation. Through contemplation, one clearly knows the object being contemplated. Thanks to contemplating the mind, one truly understands the concept of emptiness, and then reaches a state where there are absolutely no false thoughts. These six types are the An Ban Thu Intention. In the sutras, it is used again: The four thoughts are just the number of words; The four thoughts are arbitrary; The four gods are mindful of mindfulness; The five senses and five powers are contemplation; The seven senses are complete; The eight virtues are pure. It explains thoroughly about news books. By practicing these six things, you can also achieve the recitation of the Thirty-seven-Level Sutra. The An Ban Thu Y Sutra explains in detail how to practice these six things.

The An Ban Thu Y Sutra, the sutra representing the Hinayana teachings of An The Cao, was accepted very quickly by the Chinese. Taoism used this sutra to establish the 'Thai Tic' dharma.

The meaning of the An Ban Thu Y sutra.

Buddha said:

- I practiced 'An Ban Thu Y' for ninety days, and my body and mind were free. After you have finished practicing An Ban Thu Y, you can withdraw your thoughts. An is the body. Ban is breath. The intention is the way. To comply means to forbid, also called not to violate the precepts. Ban is also called household. To protect means to protect all the precepts without breaking them. The mind is the mind, it is also the way.

An Ban means breathing in and out, also the method of breathing. The method of breathing, that is, Contemplation, is the basic foundation of cultivating the Way. By following this method, one can give birth to the Tathagata's virtue. 'An Ban' follows the breathing method and becomes 'Thu'. The four meditations rely on the body to complete 'Concentration'. The Dharma of breathing has six stages: Breathing, depending, concentration, contemplation, completeness, and tranquility. People who practice meditation often have to go through four stages of meditation. Mr. Dao An clearly pointed out that the So Tic meditation and the Four Meditations are the special features of 'An Ban'.

The adoption of the 'An Ban Thu Y' sutra into the Chinese ideological culture is as follows: Humans originally live according to heaven and earth. Therefore, life depends on the loss of respiration. Respiration, or breath, is the source of life, and is also the active force of heaven and earth. If we clearly realize that the energy of respiration is constantly operating, then humans can merge with heaven and earth into one body. This Dharma is consistent with Chuang Tzu's theory. From ancient times until now, people have known how to inhale new breath and exhale old breath.

Dharma Thai That of the Chinese, invented by Taoists. In the sutras translated by An The Cao such as the An Ban Thu Y sutra and Am Tri Enter, the 'An Ban' dharma was taken advantage of by the Taoists and adapted into the 'Thai Tic' dharma.

Later, great master Tri Gia relied on the six virtues (six virtues) of the An Ban Thu Y sutra to establish 'The Six Wonderful Dharma Mon'. Indeed, the fourth part of Thien Thai Tieu Chi Quan all discusses the breathing method. Japanese Zen Master Do Nguyen, when preaching about the method of sitting meditation, also discussed the method of breathing.

Therefore, in terms of thought and practice, over many generations, the An Ban Thu Y Sutra has had a great influence on practitioners of meditation.

Representing the Dharma Sutra that An The Cao translated is the Amitabha Sutra. Including: Form, sound, scent, taste, wrong thoughts, five skandhas; The six bodies are eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind; The ten forms of input are eye, form, ear, sound, smell, smell, tongue, taste, body, and pleasure; The six minds and six consciousnesses are eye consciousness, ear consciousness, nose consciousness, tongue consciousness, body consciousness, consciousness; The four truths are suffering, cessation, and path; The thirty-seven levels of enlightenment are the four principles of mind, the four severances of mind, the four spiritual sufficiency, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven enlightened minds, and the eight types of virtue; The five faculties are the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom; The five virtues are faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; The four luxuries are the luxury of desire, the luxury of views, the luxury of vows, and the luxury of body and conduct; The three realms are the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

tom_tat: During the Eastern Han Dynasty, continuing the translation career of An The Cao, there were Chi Lau Ca Sam, An Huyen, Truc Soc Phat, Nghiem Phat Dieu,...
noi_dung:
04. LokaraksaDuring the Eastern Han Dynasty, continuing the translation career of An The Cao, there were Chi Lau Ca Sam, An Huyen, Truc Soc Phat, Nghiem Phat Dieu, etc.

During the Qin and Han dynasties, the country of Dai Nhuc Chi rampaged in Central Asia, controlling the northern regions of Afghanistan, Kien Da La, etc. The first great translator from the country of Dai Nhuc Chi to Central Earth was Mr. Chi Lau Ca Sam, or Chi Sam for short. His personality is lively and clear; All my life I practice strictly following the precepts, not going one inch beyond the precepts; diligence in reciting and reciting many sutras; All my life I have taken the aspiration to propagate Buddhism as my main responsibility.

He came to Luoyang in the final years of Han Emperor (147-167). During the reign of Emperor Linh Quang Hoa, in the Trung Binh era (178-190), he specialized in translating scriptures. However, his life biography is very simple; Even when and where he was naturalized is still unclear. According to the 'Tripitaka', Chi Sam translated thirteen sutras, and twenty-seven volumes as follows: 1/ Shurangama Sutra (2 volumes); 2/ Ban Zhou Sanmuoi (1 volume); 3/ Prajnaparamita Virtue (10 volumes); 4/ Truly Da La Ni (2 volumes); 5/ The Ancient Collection of Ancient Writings on Prajnaparamita Theory (1 volume); 6/ Bright Samadhi (1 volume); 7/ A Xa The Vuong (2 volumes); 8/ Bao Tich (1 volume); 9/ Questioning (1 volume); 10/ Ho Prajna Ne Hoan (1 volume); 11/ Suat Sa (1 volume); 12/ A Xa Buddha Kingdom (1 volume); 13/ Bo Bon (2 volumes); 14/ Internal Tripitaka (1 volume).

Venerable An The Cao mainly specializes in translating Hinayana sutras. Chi Sam's special part is specializing in translating Mahayana scriptures. The reason for this difference is because at that time, in the An Tuc country of Mr. An The Cao, Theravada Buddhism flourished, while in the country of Dai Nhuc Chi of Mr. Chi Sam, Mahayana Buddhism developed strongly. In addition, Truc Soc Phat only brought Mahayana scriptures from the Western Regions to Central Earth, then passed them on to Chi Sam to translate. The most powerful influence on posterity is the Tao Hanh Prajna Sutra translated by Mr. Chi Sam. Of course, the method of meditation in the Shurangama Sutra does not agree with An Thegao's view of meditation, because this sutra explains Mahayana meditation. Shurangama Samadhi is the sutra that Chi Sam translated first. During the Wei and Jin dynasties, Mahayana meditation was circulated, so Chi Sam's mission of translating Mahayana sutras was very important. The translator's difficulty is in applying the text. He often did not insist on elaborate prose, but only wanted to be able to translate the meaning of the sutra.

The monk who has a close relationship with Mr. Chi Sam is Mr. Truc Soc Phat. In the second year of the Han Dynasty, Quang Hoa (179), Truc Soc Phat brought the sutras to Luoyang, and together with Chi Sam embarked on the career of translating the sutras. According to historical records, on the full moon day of the ninth month in the year 179, Truc Soc Buddha orally recited the Tao Hanh Sutra and Ban Chu Sam Muoi; Mr. Chi Sam translated; The attendants were Nam Duong Truong Thieu An and Nam Hai Tu Bich. The helpers were Ton Hoa and Chu De Vi.

In addition to Mr. Truc Soc Phat, Mr. Chi Sam also has a close relationship with Mr. Chi Dieu, who is a monk of Dai Nhuc Chi country. Venerable Chi Dieu also translated a book of Sutras called the Samadhi of Light and Clearness, which is also the same as the Sutra of Illumination Samadhi translated by Venerable Chi Sam. According to Hui Kieu in the book Cao Tang Truyen, Mr. Chi Dieu translated the Anaṇa Sutra of the Eight Remembrances, Minor Paths, The Master of Clear Concentration, Ma Huu Tam General, Ma Huu Bat Thai Du Nhan, etc.

In addition, there are two translators also from Dai Nhuc Chi country to Dong Do: Chi Viet and Chi Luong. Chi Viet also called Chi Cung Minh. During the winter of Han Ling De, his father went to Central Earth, so Chi Viet was born in Dong Do. Therefore, Mr. Chi Viet soon became fluent in Chinese. Although I once met Mr. Chi Sam, I could not serve him as a teacher, but only followed Mr. Chi Sam's disciple, Chi Luong, to learn the Dharma; Perhaps because at that time Mr. Chi Sam was old or about to pass away.

Mr. Chi Viet is exceptionally talented and has profound knowledge of internal and external scriptures. Mr. Chi Viet translated the sutra very fluently, flexibly, and achieved the meaning of the sutra. Because of the chaos after the Eastern Han Dynasty, Chi Viet went south to the country of Wu. From 139 to 153, Chi Viet translated ten volumes of sutras.

During the reign of Emperor Ling of Han, he came from An Tuc country along with An The Cao, An Huyen. He was originally a lay Upasaka, with an upright personality, seriously observed the five lay precepts, and was erudite and read many scriptures. At the end of the Han Dynasty, the fourth year of Quang Hoa (181), he went to Luoyang. Because he needed someone to do business, he was assigned the position of Cavalry Captain. His personality is very gentle, and he often takes daily Buddhist practice as his duty. Gradually knowing Chinese, he made an effort to preach Buddhist scriptures, and often discussed with monks. Buddhists who practice the Mahayana religion all call him Admiral Huyen.

An Huyen once translated the Dharma Mirror Sutra with Nghiem Phat Dieu. This Dharma Mirror Sutra was read by An Huyen from Sanskrit into Chinese, then translated by Nghiem Phat Dieu, so the translation was very good, and people of later generations often praised it.

Nghiem Phat Dieu was the person who helped An Huyen translate the Dharma Mirror Sutra. Originally from Anhui, Nghiem Phat Dieu was very studious in his childhood, and was full of faith and wisdom. Later, he became a monk and became a disciple of Mr. An The Cao. According to the history of Chinese Buddhism, Master Nghiem Phat Dieu was the first Chinese person to become a monk. Nghiem Phat Dieu also often focuses on translating sutras. People at that time praised three translators: An The Cao, An Huyen, and Nghiem Phat Dieu. An Huyen praised Nghiem Buddha's translation of the sutra as follows:

- Master Nghiem Phat Dieu translates the sutra, making the reader awaken without being troubled. The translation is very clear and skillful.

Venerable Khuong Sang Hoi praised An Huyen and Nghiem Phat Dieu in the preface to the Dharma Mirror Sutra: "The two wise men Cavalry An Huyen and Lam Hoai Nghiem Buddha Dieu were in their youth, determined to spread the holy karma; their words were profound, reaching the depths of their spirit, reaching profound understanding; pitying the blind and ignorant worldly people who did not know the Great Dharma, they exhausted all their thoughts to translate this exemplary sutra. Do The story is narrated by Nghiem Phat Dieu."

During the last period of the Later Han Dynasty, among the translators, Nghiem Phat Dieu was the main focus. Master Nghiem Phat Dieu prepared the book 'Sa Di Thap Hue Chuong Cu'.

The book 'The Samaritan Thap Hua Chuong Cu' was originally translated by An The Cao and had not yet been translated, so his disciple Nghiem Phat Dieu continued to complete the translation.

In addition, during the reign of Emperor Linh De of Han, there were also translators such as Chi Dieu (a monk from Dai Nhuc Chi country), Khuong Cu (from Khuong Cu country), Khuong Manh Tuong (from Khuong Cu country). Chi Dieu translated the sutra book The City of Concentration of Intent, Small Bodhisattva, etc. in Luoyang. Khuong Cu translated the Sutra of Questions on Hell in 187; The text points directly to the original intention of the sutra, without any attempt to enhance the appearance. Khuong Manh Tuong together with Truc Dai Luc (from Thien Truc) translated Trung Bon Khoi and Dao Hanh Khoi in 199. These two Sanskrit sutras were originally requested by monk Dam Qua in the country of Ca Duy La Ve.

After the Later Han dynasty passed away, China was divided into three kingdoms: Wei, Shu, and Wu. At that time, in the north, the center of Buddhism was Luoyang. The Buddhist center in the south is Jianye (Nanjing). Those are two places that translators from Thien Truc and Tay Vuc often visit. According to the book 'Khai Nguyen Luc', the translators in the Wei country were: 1/ Mr. Dam Kha Ca La, a native of Thien Truc, came to Trung Tho during the Cao Wei dynasty, the second Gia Binh era (250); 2/ Mr. Khuong Tang Khai, from Thien Truc, came to Central Earth during the reign of Cao Wei, in the 19th year of Gia Binh (252); 3/ Mr. Dam Wu De, a native of An Xi country, came to Central Earth during the Cao Wei dynasty, the year of Chanh Nguyen Nguyen (254); 4/ Mr. Bach Dien, from the Western Regions, came to Central Earth during the Cao Wei dynasty, the third Cam Lo era (258); 5/ Mr. An Phap Hien, from the Western Regions, came to Central Earth during the Cao Wei dynasty (date unknown).

tom_tat: Dam Kha Ca La's translation of the Vinaya had a great influence on the monks in Cao Wei.
noi_dung:
05. Dharmakala (Dharmakala)Dam Kha Ca La's translation of the Vinaya had a great influence on the monks in Cao Wei.

Mr. Dam Kha Ca La in Chinese translates as Phap Thoi, came from the middle of Thien Truc, had a long-standing family history of wealthy people, and often practiced Pham Phuoc. From a young age, his talent surpassed that of ordinary people. Extensive scholarly knowledge, thorough knowledge of the four Vedas, knowledgeable about astronomy, stars, geography, fortunes, maps, and thunder. He once said:

- The literature of the world is all in My belly.

That is a word of confidence. But when I met the Buddha's teachings, those attachments all disappeared. At the age of twenty-five, he went to visit a monk at the monastery and suddenly saw the book Abhidhamma Abhidharma, so he took it and read it. Regarding this book, he was completely confused and could not understand it. Even though I read it three times, I still don't understand it clearly, so I complain:

- From the time I grow up, I only need to read all the education, classic stories, etc. once to understand the meaning, but I never read it more than three times. Today I read the Buddhist scriptures, it's beyond my understanding. The principles here are profound and must be essential.

Therefore, he took this treatise, went to the monk's room, questioned the monks, and explained the Abhidharma mysticism. After being explained, he then deeply understood the principle of cause and effect and retribution, and understood the principle of reincarnation in three lifetimes. From then on, he understood the depth and breadth of Buddhism that secular books could not match. Therefore, he decided to give up worldly glory and wealth and become a monk. He often practiced asceticism, read and recited Mahayana and Hinayana sutras as well as Bhikkhunī rules, then went to educate people.

During the reign of Emperor Cao Phe, in the second year of Gia Binh (250), he came to Luoyang. At that time, although Buddha Dharma existed, religion was in decline. Many monks, who have never taken precepts, only practice like lay people. The difference is that they shave their heads and put on robes, and often perform repentance ceremonies, festivals, or rituals. The festival was founded by So Vuong Anh or Han Hoan De. Sacrifice was originally the worship method of Hoang Lao, and then added the Buddhist worship ritual. Monks of the Cao Wei dynasty did not need to receive precepts. As for the methods of repentance, just follow the method of practice, without understanding anything about the dharma of Buddhism.

Therefore, as soon as he arrived in Lac Duong, Mr. Dam Kha Ca La advocated that all rituals must follow Buddhist regulations. Because he was well-versed in jurisprudence, the monks there asked him to translate the precepts. The meanings in the Vinaya Pitaka are very rich and complex, but Buddhism at that time was not yet flourishing. If he translated according to the Vinaya Pitaka, he was afraid that the masses would not be able to accept it, so he only translated a volume of Sangha Precepts Tam (a compendium of the precepts of the Maha Sangha Nikaya). The thirty-fifth volume of 'Buddha's Patriarch', records as follows: "In the second Gia Binh era, the Tripitaka Dharma Master Dam Kha Ca La (or Dam Ha Ca La) from Thien Truc to Luo Duong, translated the volume 'Sang Ky Gioi', and established the law of Yet Ma to receive great monk ordination. Previously, monks became monks and only shaved their hair, there was never any ritual, but only Dharma repentance as a sacrifice. When they came to Lac. Duong, Mr. Dam Kha Ca La translated it into a book of precepts to serve as a rule for daily practice for the monks."

In the past, the two monks and monks only took three refuges. There is no clear distinction between monks and novices. Therefore, Venerable Dam Kha Ca La, along with the monk of the country An That is Dam De, translated the four-part precepts of Dam Vo Duc. Next, ten Thien Truc monks together practiced the Yet Ma practice of transmitting precepts. Monk Chau Si Hanh was the first to receive precepts. Cao Tang's Tale recorded: "The precepts in the Central Earth precepts originate from here."

Therefore, in Dong Do people later honored Dam Kha Ca La as the first ancestor of Luat Tong.

Previously, An The Cao had translated books on Hinayana precepts such as: Sariputra Repentance Sutra, Samadhi of the Law Sutra, Brahman Precepts Reaction to Disdain Sutra, and Maha Bhikkhu Three Thousand Dignity Sutra (2 volumes).

Continuing Dam Kha Ca La's career of translating the Mahayana precepts were Khuong Tang Khai and Dam De.

tom_tat: Although Mr. Khuong Tang Khai (Samgaraman) is not sure where he comes from, he may be from Khuong Cu country. At the end of the Gia Binh era (253), he...
noi_dung: 06. Mr. Khuong Tang KhaiAlthough Mr. Khuong Tang Khai (Samgaraman) is not sure where he comes from, he may be from Khuong Cu country. At the end of the reign of Gia Binh (253), Mr. Khuong Tang Khai came to Luo Duong. According to the first book 'Khai Nguyen Luc', at Bach Ma Pagoda in Luoyang, Mr. Khuong Tang Khai translated the Amitabha Elder Question Sutra, the Infinite Life Sutra (2 volumes), and the Four Parts and Yet Ma. Regarding the Infinite Life Sutra, there are many different theories. The first theory is that this sutra was translated by Khuong Zeng Kai during the Cao Wei period. The second theory is that it was translated by Truc Phap Ho of the Western Jin Dynasty. The third theory is that Buddha Da Bat Da La and teacher Bao Van translated.

tom_tat: According to Cao Tang Truyen, the monk Dam De was originally from An Tuc country, came to Lac Duong during Cao Wei's reign in 254, and translated the book Dam Vo Duc...
noi_dung:
07. Dharmasatya or DharmasatyaAccording to Cao Tang Truyen, the monk Dam De was originally from An Tu, came to Lac Duong during Cao Wei's reign in 254, and translated the book Dam Vo Duc Yet Ma.

From the Eastern Han Dynasty to the Three Kingdoms, most translators specialized in translating classics. Regarding the fundamental precepts of the Sangha, few people promote and propagate them. It was not until the end of the Jin dynasty and the Cao Wei dynasty that the law was slowly translated.

In addition, there was Mr. Bach Dien from Quy Tu country, in the Cao Wei dynasty, at the end of the Chanh Thuy era, translating the Shurangama Sutra, Tu Lai Sutra, and Exorcism Brain Sutra.

According to the book 'The Great Three Jewels Calendar' by Mr. Truc Dao To, there is also the translator An Phap Hien. An Phap Hien translated the La Ma Gia Sutra (3 volumes), the Mahaparinirvana Sutra (2 volumes), and four other volumes and two books of sutras. Mr. Vo La Xoa (Moraksa), a native of the Western Regions, multi-literate and scholarly, together with the layman Truc Thuc Lan (originally from Thien Truc, following his father to flee to Ha Nam) translated the Sutra of Radiance of Light and Prajna in the reign of Nguyen Khang (291).

In addition, there were translators such as: Cuong Luong Lau Chi (Kalaruci), a native of Thien Truc, translated the sutras in Guangzhou in the year 281. Mr. An Phap Kham, a native of An Xi, translated the sutras in Luoyang from 281 to 306. Venerable Chi Phap Du, a native of Dai Nhuc Chi, translated the sutras in Luoyang in the year 301. Venerable Nha La Nghiem, a native of Thien Truc, translated the sutras in Lac Duong. Yang around the year 316.

tom_tat: His ancestors were originally from Khuong Cu country, and later settled in Thien Truc. The father migrated to Vietnam because of business...
noi_dung:
08. Mr. Khuong Tang HoiHis ancestors were originally from Khuong Cu country, and later settled in Thien Truc. Because of business, the father migrated to Vietnam (Giao Chau). Therefore, he was born in Vietnam (Giao Chau). When he was ten years old, both of his parents passed away. After the period of mourning, he resolved to become a monk. In the Sangha, he tried his best to practice, not relaxing at all. He used gentleness and courtesy to treat others. Even though he had extensive knowledge, he was always dedicated to studying. He had a thorough understanding of the three sutras, rules, and treatises. He was knowledgeable about Confucian letters, poetry, translations, rituals, spring and autumn, and other classics. In addition, in astronomy, geography, and all kinds of bibliography, He is all knowledgeable. Skilled in rhetoric, fluent in literature.

At that time, the Jiangnan region was controlled by Ngo Ton Quyen. Buddhism had just spread to that place, so its education had not yet expanded. Because of his determination to make Buddhism flourish, he came from Vietnam (Giao Chau) to Giang Nam to build a pagoda and create a Buddha statue. In the tenth year of Red Bird (247), he went to Kien Nghiep (Nanjing, the capital of the Wu Dynasty), built a thatched hermitage, established a monk's room, and created a Buddha statue.

Because Buddhism had just been introduced, people only understood Buddhism through the teachings of practicing monks. Therefore, few people understand the meaning of Buddhism, and very few people know about the practice of becoming a monk. A mandarin once told Ngo Ton Quyen:

- The Thien Truc people came from the west and called themselves monks. The appearance and clothes are different from the Chinese people. Your Highness, please examine their actions.

Ngo Ton Quyen says:

- I have heard the ancient story of Han Ming De dreaming about a god and calling him Buddha. Are the actions and movements of those monks not similar to the teachings of Buddha?

Ngo Ton Quyen later summoned him into the capital to question him:

- You monks practice Buddhism, what kind of inspiration do you get?

He said:

- The Tathagata entered nirvana more than a thousand years ago, but the relics left behind to this day still display many miraculous signs. In the past, King Ashoka built eighty-four thousand stupas to worship relics. The tower itself represents the teachings of Buddhism.

Hearing these responses, Ngo Ton Quyen thought that they were just boastful words, so he issued an order, saying:

- If you pray for relics, I will allow you to build a stupa. If there is any lie, I will punish the crime according to national law!

Hearing that, he made a deal with Ngo Ton Quyen that within seven days, he would pray for the relics. Returning to the temple, he realized that this matter was very important, related to the survival of Buddhism, so he gathered the disciples and said:

- The survival and prosperity of Buddhism depend on praying for relics. If we do not sincerely pray for relics, then I am afraid that the Buddha Dharma will be difficult to spread in this region!

Therefore, he and his disciples took a bath, cleaned the room, then placed a bronze vase on a high throne, and sincerely offered incense, praying for the Buddha's relics to appear majestically.

After seven days, there was no response, so he had to beg for another seven days. On the fourteenth day, there was no good omen. Therefore, Ngo Ton Quyen considered it a lie, so he intended to issue an order to impose a penalty, but he was determined to request a delay of another seven days. Ngo Ton Quyen approved. By the afternoon of the twenty-first day, I still hadn't seen any relics. That night, in the fifth watch, the assembly suddenly heard a jingling sound in the bronze jar. When I opened it, I saw that relics had appeared inside. The next morning, he brought the relics illuminated in five brilliant colors in a vase and presented them to Ngo Ton Quyen. All the courtiers gathered to see the relics. They only saw the wonderful five-colored light radiating from the bronze vase. Ngo Ton Quyen personally took the jar containing the relics, then poured the relics onto the bronze tray. As soon as the relics fell, the bronze tray immediately broke. Witnessing this with his own eyes, Ngo Ton Quyen was frightened, became respectful, and said:

- What a rare omen!

Then he said:

- The majestic relics don't only shine in five colors. Even if you put them in the fire, the fire won't burn. Even if you use a vajra pestle to hit it forever, you can't break it!

Hearing this, Ngo Ton Quyen placed the relics on an iron anvil, then ordered a great athlete to beat them with an iron mace. At that time, he prayed:

- Buddha Dharma has just appeared. People have just begun to admire the kindness of the righteous religion. Looking forward to showing off more magical miracles!

The great athlete continued to pound, but only saw the anvil sink, while the relics were not dented at all, and still radiated a bright light. Seeing the clear miracle, Ngo Ton Quyen praised it immensely, then ordered the tower to be built immediately. It was the first temple established in Giang Nam, called Kien So, also known as Kien Phat. Ngo Ton Quyen also renamed the land around the pagoda as Phat Da Ly. Thanks to that, Buddhism flourished.

Ngo Ton Quyen died, Ngo Lam became consul in 256. Ngo Lam was extremely autocratic, killing monks, destroying pagodas, and persecuting the beliefs of the masses. Because of his cruel behavior, Ton Lam was eventually killed, and Sun Hao ascended the throne (264-280). Like Ton Lam, Ton Hao's personality is also rough, arrogant, and abusive of power. Sun Hao ordered the destruction of many temples and pagodas. Ngo Ton Hao told his officials:

- Why are there so many Buddhist temples established? If Buddhist teachings are compatible with the scriptures, they can be practiced and preserved. If it's just a fake, it should be burned.

The courtiers then spoke up to stop him:

- The majestic power of Buddha is boundless. Buddha is not the same as other heretical gods. Mr. Khuong Tang Hoi used his sincere heart to sense the good omen, so Emperor Ngo Dai ordered the temple to be built. If you destroy it carelessly, I'm afraid you won't regret it later!

Hearing the officials' complaints, Ngo Ton Hao did not know what was wrong, so he sent minister Truong Duc to Kien So pagoda to question Mr. Khuong Tang Hoi. Being an intellectual and eloquent person, before going to the temple, Minister Truong Duc prepared dangerous questions, hoping to embarrass Mr. Khuong Tang Hoi in front of the public. However, he improvised, responded fluently, and was not at all inferior. Discussing endlessly from morning to night, Truong Duc still could not subdue him, so he had to say goodbye. As soon as he stepped out of the temple gate, Truong Duc saw a temple right next to the temple, so he asked:

- The true teachings of Buddhism have reached the minds of people. Why is that temple still located next to the pagoda, thus tainting the teachings of Buddhism?

He said:

- For example, lightning strikes and thunder explodes, causing mountains to shatter. However, lies to the deaf, who cannot hear any sound. So the problem is not whether the thunder is small or big. If all things are in harmony with heaven and earth, then even if they are thousands of miles away, there will still be signs of understanding. Because those temples and shrines do not follow the right path, even though they are close by, they cannot sense anything.

Returning, Truong Duc recounted his answers to Ngo Ton Hao, and praised him as a most talented person. Even though he heard that, Ton Hao still did not believe him, so he gathered his officials and sages at the court, then sent someone to bring him a carriage to take him to the palace to question him, hoping to humiliate him in front of the civil and military mandarins. As soon as he arrived, Ton Hao asked:

- What is the meaning of the Buddhist theory of cause and effect?

He replied:

- The wise lord uses kindness and compassion to instruct and admonish the world, and uses morality and harmony to educate and nurture all things. If the wind and rain are favorable, all good things can flourish and grow, thanks to doing good things, they will have good retribution, but if you often do evil, you will never get that. Even though no one in the world knows that they have done wrong deeds, they cannot escape the eyes and ears of heaven's net, and will be destroyed by demons and gods for the rest of their lives. If you do evil deeds that everyone knows about, you will definitely be killed by others. The I Ching says: "The accumulation of good will never return". This is a Confucian classic, but it is also similar to the teachings of Buddhism.

- This principle is true, but the Duke of Zhou and Confucius have already taught it clearly, so why do Buddha's teachings still exist?

- The theories of Zhou Cong and Confucius only discuss short-sighted things. The theory of Buddhism is mysterious, profound and subtle. Buddha often taught that if people do evil, they will fall into hell and suffer much pain, and if they often practice good deeds, they will be born in heaven and enjoy lasting peace and joy. Isn't encouraging good deeds and preventing evil deeds an important issue?

Sun Hao was questioned back by Him, but had nothing to answer, so he had to give up for now. Although he had heard the Dharma, he did not understand it at all, and did not know how to repent and change. He complained to the monks:

- Ton Hao has a rough personality. There is really no way to explain the profound and wonderful meaning of Buddha Dharma, or advise him about the karma and consequences for him to hear. His mind is still confused and confused!

One time, the guards in the royal garden dug up a golden Buddha statue several hundred meters high. When Sun Hao heard about it, he ordered them to worship the Buddha image in an impure place. On Buddha's birthday, the eighth day of the fourth month, there is often a Buddha bathing festival. On that day, Ton Hao went to the temple and intentionally defiled the Buddha statue, saying to himself: "I'm bathing the Buddha!" then laughed and joked with the courtiers. Later, Ton Hao suddenly suffered from painful and painful edema, and his vagina was also swollen, causing him to moan loudly and cry out to heaven, so he called the royal priest in for a fortune-telling. The Thai historian said:

- This is a disease caused by offending the great gods!

Ton Hao immediately sent people to pray for relief at the temples, but his condition still did not improve at all. At that time, there was a maid in the palace who was very sincere in her belief in Buddhism, so she confessed to Ton Hao:

- Please, Your Highness, please go to the temple to repent.

Feeling extremely miserable, Ton Hao still tried his best to ask the palace maid:

- Is Buddha's magic power so majestic that it is like this?

Palace lady said:

- Buddha is a great god!

Listening to the palace maid's opinion, Ton Hao ordered someone to bring out the Buddha statue that he had previously polluted, and placed it in the palace, then respectfully used incense water to purify it ten times. Next, Ton Hao offered incense to repent, knelt down, and sincerely confessed his crimes. Thanks to that, my illness has improved a lot. Ton Hao then went to the temple and asked him to preach the Dharma. He also followed his wishes and explained in detail the essential points of the law of cause and effect and the law of sin and blessing. Having personally experienced the cause and effect of retribution, Ton Hao clearly understood the instructions, was very happy, and then asked him to allow him to see the monk's precepts. He said that those precepts were only for monastics, but that lay people could not carelessly read them. However, he took out one hundred and thirty-five vows from the Karma Sutra, then divided them into two hundred and fifty, so that when walking, standing, lying, and sitting, he vowed to benefit sentient beings, and gave them to Sun Hao. Having just looked at those benevolent and compassionate prayers, Ton Hao then asked him to command the five precepts. A few days later, Ton Hao's illness completely improved. From then on, Ton Hao ordered people to repair the pagoda and changed the name of Khuong Tang Hoi's pagoda to Thien Tu pagoda. He again ordered his officials and relatives to worship Buddhism together. Thanks to personally experiencing the inspiration of cause and effect and thanks to the teachings of Mr. Khuong Tang Hoi, Ton Hao transformed his violent nature into gentleness. His consciousness was also opened.

According to the book 'Exit Tripitaka', Mr. Khuong Tang Hoi translated the following sutras: Ananda Niem Di Sutra, Kinh Face King, Sat Vi King, Pham Hoang Vuong, Dao Pham, Luc Do Tap, etc. In addition, he also annotated and composed prefaces for An Ban Thu Y Sutra, Phap Realm, Dao Tho Sutra, etc.

Mr. Dao An recorded: "In ancient times, Nghiem Phat Dioc composed the Samidhi Thap Hue Chapter Cu. The Khuong Sangha gathered together the Luc Do essentials, along with the Ngo Pham Sutra."

The Six Essential Sections of Mr. Khuong Sang Hoi still exist today: 1/ Infinite Almsgiving Chapter; 2/ Limitless Limits Chapter; 3/ Endless Patience Chapter; 4/ Endless Effort Chapter; 5/ Infinite Meditation Chapter; 6/ Minh Do Infinity Chapter. These are the six paramitas that the Buddha actually practiced for countless eons in the past.

In the sutras that he translated and annotated or wrote prefaces to, such as the An Ban Thu Y sutra, the Phap Kinh sutra, the Miscellaneous Simulations sutra, the Small Products, etc., the writing is very skillful and secretive, making everyone who reads it feel impressed. In addition, he also explained the Brahma Sutras, the King of Sat Vi, the Mirror of the King, and Ananda's Remembrance.

Mr. Khuong Tang Hoi passed away in the reign of Jin Wu De, in the reign of Taikang (280).

During the Three Kingdoms period, due to the translation and commentary of Khuong Tang Hoi, Buddhist ideas were widely circulated, and strongly influenced the practice of the masses, along with the construction of temples by Chinese monks.

Buddhism in the Eastern Han Dynasty, such as So Vuong Anh or Han Hoan De, was limited to building temples, creating Buddha statues, or practicing according to traditional rituals, and the translation of scriptures was not very developed. The beginning of the career of translating Hinayana sutras was Mr. An The Cao, and the translator of Mahayana sutras was Mr. Chi Lau Ca Sam, and the successors of this career were Mr. Khuong Tang Hoi and Chi Khiem. An The Cao's sutras on meditation and arithmetic were later inherited by An Huyen, Nghiem Phat Dieu, Nam Duong Han Lam, Danh Xuyen Bi Nghiep, Ke Tran Hue Hoi, Khuong Tang Hoi, etc.

Mr. Khuong Tang Hoi came from Vietnam and was well-versed in Chinese culture and literature, so it was natural that while translating the scriptures, he wanted to fuse Buddhist thought with Chinese thought. For example, in the preface to the An Ban Thu Y sutra, Khuong Tang Hoi uses a lot of Lao Trang's terms.

Thanks to the two great translators An The Cao and Chi Khiem, the Hinayana teachings were widely circulated. In addition, the Mahayana Prajnaparamita teachings were initiated by two great translators, Chi Lau Ca Sam and Khuong Tang Hoi.

Although his parents were originally from Khuong Cu, Mr. Khuong Tang Hoi was born and raised in Vietnam (Giao Chau). Therefore, unlike the monks from Thien Truc, Tay Vuc, etc., Mr. Khuong Tang Hoi was originally Vietnamese, became a monk, attained enlightenment, lit the torch of Zen Buddhism and Mahayana teachings in Vietnam, then led his disciples to spread Buddhism right in China. Thanks to his efforts, Buddhism in Jiangnan region flourished. Therefore, Khuong Zeng Hoi's work in spreading Buddhism had a great influence on the history of Chinese Buddhism. The torch of Dharma passed on by him will forever shine in the minds of the Chinese people. Of course, his reputation and virtue have highlighted the history of Vietnamese Buddhism. He is the representative of many other high-ranking monks in Vietnam who went to Central Vietnam to spread the Dharma and teach the religion to the kings and Chinese people, such as the shaman Phung Dinh (who came to preach the sutras in the Tang king's palace), the shaman Duy Giam (who came to preach the sutras in the Tang king's palace), etc. Indeed, thanks to the terrain, Buddhism was introduced to Vietnam earlier than China. This is clearly demonstrated by the book History of Vietnamese Buddhism:

"The Luy Lau center (in Giao Chau) was established the earliest and this center served as a springboard for the establishment of the Pengcheng and Luoyang centers in China."

Talking about the terrain, during the long years of darkness under domination, Vietnam (Giao Chau) was the most important trading port of the northern empire from the Pre-Han Dynasty to the Tang Dynasty (111 B.C. - 907 A.D.). According to Master Thich Dong So in the book Chinese Buddhist Communication History, the trade between China and India in the centuries before and after the Western era went through three main routes: The first was along the silk route, that is, from India, over Thong Linh mountain, going east, through countries in Tay Vuc such as Ke Tan, Vu Dien, across the deserts, then entering Co Tang or Luong Chau, to reach Truong An or Lac. Duong. On the mainland, this is the route most often used by Indian monks. The second is from India, passing through Burma, then entering Yunnan. However, very few people use this route. Third is the sea route. Originating from the Indian Ocean, monks from India or the Western Regions often followed merchant ships to Vietnam (Giao Chau), before entering China. In addition, countries in the South China Sea such as Funan (Cambodia), Lion (Ceylon), etc. and even the Roman Empire, if they wanted to trade with the Chinese, first went to Vietnam (Giao Chau) by sea, and then went to the mainland. According to the storybook about Thien Truc and Tay Vuc in the Later Han Dynasty (Late Han Thu Tay Vu Thien Truc Truyen), it is written: "During the reign of Emperor Hoa De (79-104), the Thien Truc and Tay Vu countries often sent envoys to bring tribute to Nhat Nam."

The fourth book of Dai Qin stories writes: "The country of Dai Qin (China) once traded with each other by sea with the country of An Tuc and Thien Truc, both of which had benefits. Merchants and envoys often brought ivory, rhino horn, etc. to Nhat Nam."

Nhat Nam means the two provinces of Quang Binh and Quang Tri of Vietnam today. The Book of Geography of Tang, that is, the geography book of the Tang Dynasty (618-907), wrote: "Envoys and merchants from countries in the Hainan region, located to the south and southwest of Giao Chi, or five miles, five thousand miles, hundreds of thousands of miles away. They often used merchant ships to carry goods for exchange, or tribute offerings, and all came to the trading port at Giao Chi, from the reign of Emperor Wu of Han (206 B.C. TL) so far."

Furthermore, according to Sylvain and Pelliot's research, when the Chinese and Indians traded with each other, they used Vietnam (Giao Chau) as an intermediary from 245 BC to the seventh century.

In addition, at that time the Cham people were still strong, and they were deeply influenced by Indian culture. They often use books in Sanskrit, and are fluent in Quawa (Java). Vietnamese people live close to them, so of course there are many people who are fluent in Sanskrit and Chinese. Therefore, missionary groups from India often turned to Vietnamese people to ask them to interpret or translate Sanskrit scriptures into Chinese. They also often went there to learn Chinese and then began translation work. Therefore, it is not surprising that many old translations of the sutras are often translated in Vietnam.

Therefore, thanks to Indian monks continuously spreading Dharma to the Far East during the Northern colonial period, Buddhism in early Vietnam was directly influenced by Indian Buddhism. Typically, at the beginning of the first century, Indian monks from Mahayana Buddhist centers on the east coast of India such as Nagarunakonda and Amaravati often followed merchant ships to Southeast Asia. If you want to spread Buddhism into China, then of course you have to go to Vietnam (Giao Chau) first, and then go to the mainland. Upon arriving, they translated the scriptures, established a sangha, and then slowly spread Buddhism to China and Korea.

Therefore, with a favorable terrain, Vietnam soon received genuine Buddhism transmitted directly from Indian monks during the northern colonial period from the Pre-Han Dynasty to the Tang Dynasty, then used the vitality and mystery of Buddhism as a spiritual refuge, rather than being assimilated by the Confucian - Strong dogma of the Northerners into slavery like other peoples. Not only were they not assimilated, but the Vietnamese monks brought the torch of Dharma to the Chinese court.

In addition, during the three periods of Northern domination (111 p.TL - 39 a.S.TL, 43-544, 603-939), in Vietnam there were many high-ranking monks who went to Thien Truc to seek Buddha Dharma, such as Zen master Van Ky, Mr. Moc Xoa De Ba, shaman Khuy Chong, shaman Hue Diem, and shaman Giai Thoa Thien. Furthermore, Chinese monks also often come to Vietnam (Giao Chau) to board boats to Thien Truc and Tay Vuc to seek Dharma, typically monks Hue Manh, Dam Nhuan, Tri Hoang, etc.

In general, thanks to absorbing the essence of Buddhism, especially meditation, from the time Khuong Tang Hoi expounded the An Ban Thu Y meditation sutra, until Zen master Ty Ni Da Luu Chi (?-602) spread and founded Zen Buddhism, the thoughts of the Vietnamese people have always been trained with a strong will to independence. This was the key point in cultivating and cultivating the sense of autonomy and independence of the Vietnamese people during many years of being dominated by the northern empire, and then, when the opportune moment came, regaining sovereignty in 939.

Typically, thanks to absorbing the essence of Buddhism, in Vietnam, talented and virtuous monks were soon born, such as Ngo Chan Luu, Van Hanh, Phap Thuan, etc. They supported and served as military advisors to wise men such as Dinh Tien Hoang, Le Dai Hanh, Ly Thai To to steer the national ship out of the muddy land of slavery, regain sovereignty and independence for the nation, and then build benevolent dynasties. and the most prosperous in the country's history, throughout the four dynasties of Dinh, Le, Ly, and Tran (939-1400).
